title: Generative AI is becoming a cultural-representation problem: identity, sacred meaning, and local red lines shape acceptable use
source_unit: Google Research preprint, Cultural Perspectives and Expectations for Generative AI: A Global Survey Approach
geography: Brazil, Cameroon, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Nigeria, South Korea, United Arab Emirates, and United States

denominator.unit: adults surveyed across 13 countries; Cameroon sample was smaller than the other country samples

cross_cultural_scope.unit: surveyed national contexts across Europe, North and South America, Asia, and Africa

culture_definition.value: The study combines closed-ended comparisons with open-ended accounts of culture, artifacts, identities, and unacceptable representations

governance_problem.value: Generative AI representation requires culturally grounded participation and sensitivity beyond a simple geography-only model of culture

observations.method: Cross-sectional, quota-oriented multi-country survey with open-ended and standardized items; the analysis uses descriptive aggregate statistics and inductive thematic analysis, with weighting described in the preprint.
observations.uncertainty: This is a preprint and the country samples are not uniformly sized; the study is not a representative global sample, does not estimate model behavior directly, and cannot establish that expressed expectations produce safer or more culturally accurate systems.
observations.subgroup: Adults familiar with or exposed to generative AI across 13 national contexts, with different languages, religions, traditions, histories, digital infrastructures, and minority or majority identities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cross-country differences may reflect translation, sample composition, current events, question framing, or uneven familiarity with generative AI rather than stable cultural boundaries.

religion_tradition.unit: percent selecting religion and tradition among their three most important cultural identities

nationality.unit: percent selecting nationality among their three most important cultural identities

ethnicity_tribe.unit: percent selecting ethnicity or tribe among their three most important cultural identities

identity_implication.value: Cultural identity is not reducible to country labels; religion, tradition, ethnicity, language, heritage, artifacts, and lived social practice can carry distinct representational stakes

observations.method: Weighted descriptive analysis of respondents selecting three culturally important social identities, supplemented by open-ended cultural definitions and examples.
observations.uncertainty: The percentages describe selection within this survey instrument and sample; they do not measure the full importance of identities, intra-country disagreement, or how identities interact in specific AI outputs.
observations.subgroup: Respondents across different national, religious, ethnic, linguistic, historical, and socioeconomic contexts; particularly communities whose cultural markers are frequently represented by external systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: The prominence of religion or tradition in a closed-ended list may partly reflect the available categories and does not mean all members of a country share the same cultural hierarchy.

observations.period: 2024-2025 survey; familiarity and use of generative AI

genai_familiarity.unit: percent reporting at least some familiarity with generative AI

active_generation.unit: percent of respondents aware of generative AI who reported actively using it to generate content

regional_variation.value: Familiarity was highest in South Korea and the UAE and lowest in France and Cameroon in the source comparison

adoption_boundary.value: High awareness does not remove uncertainty about whether generative AI can represent identity and culture authentically

observations.method: Descriptive comparison of self-reported familiarity and generative-AI use across the multi-country survey sample.
observations.uncertainty: Familiarity and use are self-reported, timing predates publication, and country differences may reflect infrastructure, language, recruitment, or policy context; no longitudinal adoption path is estimated.
observations.subgroup: Current and prospective generative-AI users with unequal access, language coverage, institutional exposure, and experience of AI-mediated cultural representation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater familiarity can increase both confidence and critical scrutiny; lower familiarity may reflect access constraints rather than lower cultural concern.

observations.period: 2024-2025 survey; cultural red lines for generative-AI representation

denominator.unit: surveyed countries used for cross-country red-line comparison

redline_prevalence.value: More than 20% of participants in every surveyed country, and often more than 30%, said some aspects of their culture should never be represented by generative AI

primary_harm.value: Inaccurate information was identified as the leading perceived threat to cultural representation

sensitive_domains.value: Religion and tradition, sacred practices, historical trauma, personal privacy, human dignity, and culturally meaningful art or music recur as sensitive domains

governance_route.value: Cultural safety requires participatory design, attention to specific identity dimensions, and mechanisms for local communities to define boundaries and contest harmful representation

observations.method: Descriptive cross-country analysis plus inductive thematic analysis of open-ended responses about culturally important and prohibited AI representations.
observations.uncertainty: A stated red line is not a legal prohibition, a stable preference, or proof that a model will produce harm; the study does not test remedies, moderation, consent, or downstream cultural effects.
observations.subgroup: People and communities whose identities, sacred meanings, historical memories, and creative practices may be represented or transformed by generative systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some culturally sensitive representation may be welcomed when communities authorize it, context is preserved, attribution is clear, and people have meaningful control or recourse.

related_sources.claim: Open-access preprint PDF containing the survey methodology, country sample, weighting description, tables, qualitative themes, and recommendations.
ArXiv landing page with title, authors, date, abstract, and license metadata.

boundary: This record adds a global cultural-governance layer for generative AI: identity, sacred meaning, historical memory, representation, participation, and redress. It is a cross-sectional preprint survey and qualitative synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a representative global census, an audit of model outputs, a legal rule, a causal study of cultural harm, or proof that any proposed safeguard works.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Open-access arXiv preprint PDF reviewed for the 13-country sample, 5,629 respondents, identity salience, generative-AI familiarity and use, regional variation, cultural red lines, perceived harms, and governance recommendations.
